title: Paycheck
full_review:
It is apropos that the best word to describe "Paycheck" (Paramount), John Woo's new sci-fi action thriller about a high-tech genius with a memory lapse problem, is "forgettable." Despite an intriguing premise based on a story by cyber-pulp icon Philip K. Dick, the film never kicks into gear thanks to its miscast lead, uncharacteristically rote direction by Woo, and preposterous plot twists which test the suspension of disbelief generally accorded the genre.

Ben Affleck stars as hired tinker Michael Jennings, an engineering wizard who specializes in pirating cutting-edge technology before it hits the market and selling it -- usually in an upgraded form -- to competing corporations. After each hush-hush job he has his brain scanned and any memories associated with the project systematically erased to prevent him from divulging company secrets.

Though well paid for his services, Jennings agrees to the ever-fateful "one last job," offered by a reptilian corporate honcho named Rethrick (Aaron Eckhart), which will set him up comfortably for life to the tune of $92 million. The only catch is that this job involves Orwellian technology so supersecret that it will cost Jennings three years of his life, and consequently three years worth of memories.

Upon successfully completing his mission, Jennings comes out of the memory deletion process only to learn that in addition to forfeiting his eight-digit paycheck -- for reasons he can't remember, of course -- he is now a target in the cross hairs of federal agents (who accuse him of stealing experimental government technology) as well as a squad of Rethrick's assassins.

Without any recollections of the intervening three years, Jennings, who for some unexplained reason is also proficient in hand-to-hand combat skills, must piece together his past using only an envelope of innocuous items (including a paper clip and a transit card) which he had the foresight to mail to himself, and which serve as a bread-crumb trail through the narrative's labyrinthine maze of plot twists. Assisting him in putting the jigsaw puzzle together is a beautiful biologist (Uma Thurman) at Rethrick's think tank, to whom Jennings discovers he is engaged to be married.

Much of the allure of Dick's futuristic flights of fancy is his ability to ground his stories in the real and the identifiable. Many of the more successful screen re-imaginings of Dick's works -- such as "Minority Report" (2002), "Total Recall" (1990) and "Blade Runner" (1982) -- involve ordinary characters entangled in extraordinary circumstances, and usually tackle big, philosophical questions like "What is it to be human?" and "What is free will?" Yet, while "Paycheck" follows suit, exploring the Promethean consequences of technology unfettered by ethics, the moral dimensions are not integrated into the narrative as well as in the aforementioned Dick-inspired films.

As witnessed in "Sum of All Fears" (2002) and "Daredevil" (2003), Affleck proves once again that, while possessing a likable charm, he is unconvincing as the heroic lead -- though after his "Gigli" debacle (a memory all would gladly have erased) his credibility as a romantic lead is equally dubious. Thurman matches Affleck's mediocrity splendidly. In addition to Eckhart, the talents of Paul Giamatti, Colm Feore and Michael C. Hall are wasted on cameos and plot-placeholder roles.

Woo, who can usually get by with a shaky narrative by dazzling viewers with his superstylized action sequences, seems to have directed this one on autopilot, with its tedious parade of the uninspired shootouts and chases lacking any trace of his signature visual flair. The film does offer some brief clever moments involving the brainy Jennings using his noggin to thwart his pursuers, but they are few and far between and ultimately subsumed by the filmmaker's predisposition to pyrotechnics.

By the end credits, viewers may be lining up to have the previous two hours erased from their memory. Word to the wise -- don't waste your paycheck.

Due to recurring action violence and brief crude language, the USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is A-III -- adults. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is PG-13 -- parents are strongly cautioned. Some material may be inappropriate for children under 13.
